Within it, compassion arises perfectly and pervades the entire dharma-realm; it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, with no sentient capacity to which it does not respond.

If one wishes to explain this in detail for easy understanding: by means of thirteen samādhis, one is rescued from the swords and staves of karmic retribution; by means of twenty-four samādhis, one is rescued from the swords and staves of the three poisons; by means of twenty-five samādhis, one is rescued from the swords and staves of afflictions that enter into emptiness; by means of twenty-five samādhis, one is rescued from the swords and staves of ignorance regarding the provisional; and by means of twenty-five samādhis, one is rescued from the swords and staves of ignorance regarding the Middle Way. Thus, all are simultaneously granted liberation.
Fifth, the perils of ghosts (*preta*) are also threefold:
first, the word-by-word commentary; second, the application of scriptural evidence; and third, contemplative understanding.
The word-by-word commentary consists of four parts:
First, the designation of the location; second, the clarification that encountering calamity is itself suffering; third, the invocation of the name is itself wholesome; fourth, the response.
Regarding the phrase "filling the three thousandfold world system," this is a figurative expression.
If one says it is "full," from where else could it have come?
Know that this is merely a figurative expression.
Why then do you not likewise figuratively assume that water or fire fills the great trichiliocosm?
Because ghosts possess mind and consciousness, they are "full" due to their mutual extension; this is a provisional assumption for the sake of convenience.
Water and fire lack mind, so [the argument] is posited as a difficulty.

As for why ghosts fear, it is because Avalokiteśvara possesses both majesty and benevolence. If it is not out of gratitude, then it must be out of fear of his majesty; thus, even upon hearing his name, they cannot cast an evil eye, much less entertain a harmful intent.
Both the malevolent mind and the evil eye have ceased. Next, regarding the proof by means of phenomena, and subsequently regarding the proof through contemplative understanding:

if one were to argue that ghosts cause affliction based on the theory of karmic retribution, then beings in the hell realm should likewise be tormented by wicked and powerful ghosts; within the ghost realm itself, those of great power would torment lesser ghosts; ghosts in the animal realm would also devour animals; and the same can be understood for the human realm. Since the various heavens govern the ghosts, how could they possibly be afflicted by ghosts?
As it is said in the Āgamas:

"A powerful ghost suddenly sat upon the throne of Śakra. Śakra became greatly enraged, but the ghost's radiance grew even more intense. When Śakra instead gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness, the ghost's radiance vanished and he departed."
"If even the Lord of Devas is thus afflicted by ghosts, how much more so the Four Heavenly Kings and those in the realm of Asuras?
In such places, where there is the terror of demonic harassment, if one invokes Avalokiteśvara, they can no longer inflict harm."
Next, to clarify the cultivation of causes: there are those who possess evil karma and are thus called "ghosts" (bhūta), and these ghosts themselves stir up the three poisons.
As the *Āgama* states: "There are also ghosts of lust;
when a ghost enters a person's mind, it causes them to engage in unrestrained lewdness. Or the ghost may incite anger or incite depravity; one should know that ghosts likewise destroy goodness."

Regarding the statement that "the three poisons are themselves demons": lust destroys the Brahma-conduct; hatred destroys compassion; the demon of greed afflicts the precept against stealing; and the demon of craving afflicts the precept against drinking. This applies even to the ten wholesome actions and the various dhyānas; all are damaged by the demons of evil karma, which destroy the moving and non-moving karmas of humans and devas. If one can invoke [the Buddha's] name, these demons will no longer inflict harm.

Next, to clarify the demons of affliction: the mind that perceives is the male demon, and the mind that craves is the female demon. If one were to discuss these demons, they would fill the entire trichiliocosm; this is no mere figurative expression.

Why is this? Because there are eighty-eight latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) throughout the three realms, and ninety-eight latent tendencies of craving (*tṛṣṇā-anuśaya*) throughout the three realms; how could they not be all-pervasive?
This ghost intends to come and harass those of the Two Vehicles, as well as practitioners of the Six Paramitas, the Shared, Distinct, and Complete Teachings.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One, the virtuous and skillful master of incantations, will eliminate for us the ghosts of ignorance."
Furthermore, it is said:
"The rākṣasa of ignorance dwells therein. Is this not the demon of affliction?

If one recites its name and maintains mindfulness, the wisdom of contemplation will be perfected; thus, one can cause the dust and toil of views and craving to turn according to one's will, so that they cannot cause harm.

Next, regarding the distinct and perfect fundamental contemplation on compassion as the response to the capacity of sentient beings: when a Bodhisattva of the distinct teaching first resolves his mind, he sees various evil spirits tormenting and disturbing the world, with no one able to rescue or liberate them—just as the Kṛtāntakas and others tormented Vaiśālī. For this reason, the Bodhisattva gives rise to compassion and provides protection for them. Furthermore, if those who cultivate various virtues are destroyed by evil, he likewise gives rise to compassion so that their goodness may be brought to fulfillment.

If one contemplates that these ghosts and karma-ghosts are all phenomena produced by causes and conditions—entering emptiness from the provisional, and entering the Middle Way from the provisional—one should, at every stage, cultivate compassion and make vows. By profoundly penetrating the true mark (*dharmatā*) within all afflictions, one achieves the King Samādhi and perfumes the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm through the power of these vows. If one encounters the calamity of ghosts, one can provide universal protection throughout the Dharma-realm: using the compassion of phenomenal practice to rescue those ghosts who are the fruit of retribution; using the compassion of cultivated goodness to rescue those ghosts of evil karma; and using the compassion of the three contemplations to rescue those ghosts of craving, views, and ignorance. Thus, all ghosts are made capable of being mounted and controlled, such that they cannot look upon one with an evil eye.
As stated in the forty-third fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"In the city of Kapilavastu, after sunset, the night goddess Saṃpūrṇa beheld from within the void that upon her body all the stars were manifest within a single pore; she saw the sentient beings she transformed, some being born in the heavens, some attaining the two vehicles, and others practicing the bodhisattva path—she saw and heard all these various skillful means."
At that time, the Night Goddess said to Sudhana:

"I give rise to great loving-kindness toward evil sentient beings, and great compassion toward those who are unwholesome. Toward śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, I give rise to the mind that establishes them in the path of all-knowledge. Seeing sentient beings who have strayed from the right path, entered upon deviant tracks, are attached to various inversions, are deluded by falsehoods, and undergo manifold sufferings—having seen this, I employ immeasurable skillful means to eliminate their various deviant delusions and establish them in right view."
Thus we know that Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, by means of yakṣa and ghostly bodies, are able to establish sentient beings in such a manner.
How could the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara not be thoroughly proficient in this dharma-gate of ghosts and spirits, universally responding to all so that they may attain freedom from harm?

If one contemplates the seeds of consciousness as the gate of the love-and-view ghosts, then all dharmas approach this seed of consciousness as the dharma-gate of ghosts; the ten dharma realms and the three truths are fully present within it, and impartial compassion universally covers all beings—this is precisely the power of the King Samādhi of the Ghost Gate, responding everywhere throughout the dharma realm.

If explained in detail: by means of thirteen samādhis, one saves the ghosts who perform rituals; by means of twenty-four samādhis, one saves the ghosts of evil karma; and by means of twenty-five samādhis, one saves the ghosts of those of the Two Vehicles who have entered the emptiness of the Shared, Distinct, and Complete Teachings, up until their entry into the Middle Way; at all times, none of these are harmed.
Sixth, the difficulty regarding shackles and fetters also consists of three parts:
first, the word-by-word commentary (*tiwen*); second, the citation of scriptural evidence; and third, the interpretive exposition.
The word-by-word commentary consists of four sections:
First, the designation of whether one is guilty or innocent; second, encountering calamity; third, calling upon the name; fourth, the response.

When one is about to suffer harm and is certain to enter the category of death, this clarifies whether there is guilt or innocence—whether the investigation has not yet been finalized, or whether a judgment for penal servitude or exile can be made. Whether the judgment has been rendered or not, both are subject to confinement; this clarifies that the Sage’s mind is fundamentally equal in its intent to rescue those held in captivity, regardless of whether they are guilty or innocent.

Those on the hands are called cangues; those on the feet are called fetters; those on the neck are called collars; and those that encircle the body are called chains—these are the names for the three types of wooden restraints and one type of iron restraint.

"Binding" (saṃyojana) means being bound and obstructed; "restraint" (nigraha) refers to confinement. One who is bound is not necessarily restrained, but one who is restrained is inevitably bound. When one is both bound and fully restrained, anxiety and fear are likewise profound.
When a bird dies its cry is mournful, and when a person dies their words are virtuous; yet if one can invoke Avalokiteśvara, heavy gates open of their own accord and iron and wood break asunder.
To cite further evidence from historical accounts, the *Yingyan zhuan* states: "Gaihu was a native of Shanyang who was imprisoned and facing execution.

For three days and three nights his mind remained without ceasing [in devotion], whereupon he saw with his own eyes Avalokiteśvara emitting light that shone upon him. His shackles fell off and the prison door opened; following the light, he departed, and it was only after traveling twenty li that the radiance finally faded."

Zhang Chang served as the Chief Secretary to Prince Xiao of Qiao. When both the Prince and Zhang were imprisoned by the Court of Judicial Review, [Hui]song recited the sutras one thousand times; the shackles broke inch by inch, and before long they were all gone. The Grand Chancellor [Xie An] remarked on this, saying, "How extraordinary!"

3. Regarding the explanation of the contemplation: The essence of hell is imprisonment; ghosts and animals likewise suffer confinement and captivity; even the asuras are bound by the five fetters. While those in the northern continent and the heavens may enjoy sovereignty and thus seem free from such hardship, once they descend from those realms, none can escape the calamities of the dark prison. Yet, if one can invoke the Name, all shall attain its severance and destruction.
Next, the cultivation of causes is explained: evil karma is termed a "shackle. Although various karmas possess power, they do not pursue one who does not create them;
yet if one creates karma, its fruit will ultimately never be lost. Therefore, it is said that the non-perishing dharma is like a promissory note.

If a person cultivates various virtues but is shrouded by evil karma—like a great mountain casting its shadow over the mind—it causes their goodness to perish and further increases their evil karma; this evil karma then brings about the bonds of its retribution, from which there is no way to escape.
If one wishes to be liberated from these karmic actions, they can be saved during the causal stage; by urgently invoking Avalokiteśvara, one can cause the three evil karmas to be destroyed.

Thus, the Sūtra says: "Wives and children serve as shackles and fetters; wealth serves as a prison; and royal law serves as the prison register. These obstruct the practitioner so that they cannot cultivate the Way. Viewed in the present, these are the bonds of retribution; viewed in the past, they are karma."
Next, regarding the clarification of the śrāvakas: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those who have attained the first three fruits are all possessed of fault, whereas the arhat is without fault.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"The mahānāgas, whether they possess faults or are without fault, are alike within the prison of the triple world, bound by the ropes of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and constrained and sealed by the three marks of impermanence."

The delusions regarding the provisional and the real are called "handcuffs"; the delusions regarding meditative concentration and wisdom are called "fetters"; the delusions regarding the Middle Way are called "collars"; and the delusions regarding the Dharma-body are called "shackles. Bound by such things, the practitioner cannot attain liberation; yet by invoking the name and maintaining mindfulness, one will surely receive spiritual response.

If one gives rise to concentration and wisdom, the shackles are severed; if one gives rise to the provisional and the real, the cangues are severed; if one destroys ignorance, the collar is severed; if the Dharma-body manifests, the fetters are severed; if one enters nirvana without remainder, the bonds are severed; to escape the three marks is to leave the interrogation; to exit the triple world is to leave the prison. Furthermore, these possess both general and specific meanings.

Next, we clarify the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) practiced by Pratyekabuddhas in their shared and distinct aspects within the Perfect Teaching. If one discusses them as fetters, they still constitute the obstruction of the "earth" stage.

The meaning of the compassion arising from the fundamental contemplation of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, which responds universally to all beings, is no different from what was explained previously.

If the trichiliocosm represents the element of space, and kings, thieves, ghosts, and the like represent the element of consciousness, then regarding these ten instances of universal correspondence, this is also as previously discussed in the analysis of the fundamental contemplation.

Now it shall be explained: when Bodhisattvas perceive that sentient beings, having attained the fruit-body through emptiness and consciousness (*śūnyatā-vijñāna*), are instead afflicted by that very emptiness and consciousness; and when practicing various virtues, the karma of emptiness and consciousness can likewise destroy those virtues—thus observing that emptiness and consciousness possess both obstacles to the Three Truths and the principles of the Three Truths—they give rise to compassion at every stage. Through compassion, they desire to extract sentient beings from suffering;
through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they desire to bestow happiness upon sentient beings.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva contemplates that the four great elements, the element of space, and the element of consciousness are all empty of emptiness.

Being without the four great elements, without space, and without consciousness constitutes entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality and the attainment of the Sovereign Samādhi. Thus, one is able to manifest responsive transformations throughout the ten dharma-realms: using the compassion of phenomenal deeds to rescue those in distress within the empty consciousness of karmic retribution; using the compassion of cultivating goodness to rescue those in distress within the empty consciousness of evil karma; and using the compassion of the three contemplations to rescue those in distress within the empty consciousness of afflictions. Therefore, we know that Avalokiteśvara has attained mastery in the Dharma-gate of empty consciousness.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 39, states:
"The Bhikṣu Sunetra performs great Buddha-work within the void.

If one practices the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*), observing that the causes, conditions, nature, characteristics, beginning, end, and ultimate reality of emptiness are all equal, then all ten dharma realms will entirely enter the gate of emptiness.
Consciousness is also like this:
when it gives rise to objectless compassion and permeates all sentient beings, if there is a responsive capacity within the ten dharma realms, then all can attain liberation simultaneously.
Seventh, the difficulty of hostile bandits is also treated in three parts:
first, the word-by-word commentary; second, the citation of scriptural evidence; and third, the interpretive exposition.
The word-by-word commentary consists of four sections:
First, indicating the place of the calamity; second, indicating the person who encounters the calamity; third, clarifying the presence of the capacity [to respond];
fourth, clarifying the response. Regarding the place of the calamity: first, the location is clarified, which is the great trichiliocosm.
Next, the objection is clarified: "the country is filled with hostile bandits.
The phrase "filled with" is a hypothetical expression.
That the land is vast and the bandits numerous, yet the power of the Sage can still rescue them, demonstrates the ultimate extent of his merit.
Regarding "enemies," this difficulty is particularly grave.
While a robber’s primary aim is wealth and an enemy’s primary aim is to take one's life, when an enemy acts as a robber, they surely plot against both wealth and life.

If those who shed blood in the past are called enemies and those who seize property in the present are called robbers, and if [the Bodhisattva] can protect even when such enemies and robbers fill the great trichiliocosm, how could he not rescue those who are less formidable?
Second, identifying the person who encounters the disaster refers to the merchant leader.
This is further divided into four parts:
first, the leader; second, having followers; third, carrying treasures; and fourth, traversing dangerous terrain.

"Merchant" (*śreṣṭhin*) means one who measures; such a person discerns value and price, is skilled in understanding profit and interest, and excels at deliberating to find what is appropriate, making him fit to be the leader of merchants.
Once there is a merchant-leader, there will likewise be commanders.
Since these merchants have already traversed perilous and distant lands, the goods they carry must necessarily be rare commodities; hence, they are called "precious treasures.

As for the "perilous road," it may refer to a path that is desolate, remote, and narrow, which is termed a perilous road, or it may refer to a place where hostile bandits emerge to attack, which is termed a perilous road.
The "conditions" (pratyaya) are also fourfold, explained first as follows:
first, consolation by others; second, exhortation to recite the name; third, praise of virtues; and fourth, the collective recitation by the multitude.
That by which they are comforted is to cease their terror;
that by which they are exhorted to invoke the name is to establish the supreme strategy;
that by which their virtues are praised is to encourage them to steady their resolve.

If one is not comforted, they will become terrified, frantic, and bewildered; although comforting them may stop their fear, if one does not devise a plan, what benefit is there in comforting them in vain?
Therefore, I exhort you to recite the Name.

Although one is exhorted to recite the name, if one does not extol the virtues and contemplate the design [of the Buddha], the mind will not be settled and the spirit will not be courageous; therefore, one must extol the virtues.

Thus we know that this Bodhisattva is certainly able to bestow fearlessness, providing a definitive refuge. This is an illustration of the many by means of the few.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

Those with great ignorance paint all manner of false views; they deny cause and effect and slander the Mahāyāna.

The faults and afflictions of the three poisons are thus; because one desires to be free from them, by maintaining mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara with utmost sincerity, one shall attain liberation. Some explain it thus:
"The alternation between rising and subsiding is termed 'liberation' (li), not the liberation that consists in total extinction."
Now, since the scriptural text speaks of detachment, for what reason do you say it is not so?
If one relies on the *Avalokana-sūtra*, it says:
"If one purifies the roots of the three poisons, there is no doubt that one will attain the Buddha-way."
Now, ten sections are composed to clarify the salvation from the three poisons:
three sections concern the suppression of delusions and the discourse on detachment, while seven sections concern the severance of delusions and the discourse on detachment.
Question:
"To be free from afflictions one must have wisdom; yet if one merely recites [the name], how can one be freed? Answer:

The sutras state that "constant mindfulness" is itself "right mindfulness. To realize that the nature of afflictions is non-existent, and to abide at the limit of desire—which is the limit of reality—is to transcend the four propositions, being neither capable nor possessed. The nature of such mindfulness is pure. If this right mindfulness is not wisdom, where else could one seek wisdom?
This wisdom is not separate from afflictions; who then could be separate from them?

If it must be as you argue—that a distinct application is required for wisdom to destroy afflictions—then there would be afflictions to be severed and a wisdom capable of severing them. However, it is not merely that afflictions cannot be severed, but that wisdom itself becomes an affliction; how, then, can this be called "wisdom that severs afflictions"?
Now, this right mindfulness does not contemplate by means of form, nor does it contemplate by means of non-form—these are four propositions;
it also contemplates by means of form, and also contemplates by means of non-form—these are likewise four propositions;

or there is the non-contemplation of sequential discourse, or the non-contemplation of non-sequential discourse; or the contemplation of non-sequential discourse, or the contemplation of sequential discourse; or the discourse on detachment in sequence, or the discourse on detachment without sequence.

Next, regarding the interpretation through contemplation (*guan-jie*), the seven stages may be understood by analogy with what precedes; here, however, they are formulated according to the two principles of progression (*shun*) and regression (*ni*) based on the realm beyond (*jie-wai*), rather than taking the characteristics of the three poisons (*san-du*) of the fragmented existence (*fen-duan*).
Now, taking the mind of wholesome desire and naming it greed, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"All wholesome dharmas have desire as their root. For those of the Two Vehicles, desiring the bliss of nirvana is called greed; loathing birth-and-death is called hatred; and failing to penetrate this principle is called ignorance. When these three poisons are opened up, the eighty-four thousand [afflictions] are perfectly and completely present.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"As long as the habitual tendencies of the fetters (*saṃyojana-vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers will cling to the body. This refers to the fact that the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) have not yet severed these three poisons; it is precisely the manifestation of the three poisons in their state of transformation (*pariṇāmika*).

Bodhisattvas who have not yet severed their individual afflictions likewise possess these three poisons; therefore it is said that a Bodhisattva greedily seeks the Buddha-dharma, never relinquishing it for even a moment throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This insatiability in extensive learning is the characteristic of greed.

Because one despises the two vehicles and takes no pleasure in hearing their names, it is said: "It would be better to give rise to the mind of a wicked, leper-like jackal than to give rise to the mind of the two vehicles.
Is this not, like the analogy of a great tree breaking its branches, a manifestation of anger?

The layers of ignorance are exceedingly numerous; they can be severed by the wisdom of the Buddha’s Bodhi. All those who have not yet fully realized the Buddha-nature possess the characteristic of delusion.
To eliminate these three afflictions, one should constantly recollect Avalokiteśvara; he will respond according to their capacities, and one shall thereby attain eternal liberation.
There are two kinds of permanent departure:
if this bodhisattva has not yet entirely eliminated the specific afflictions within the birth-body, they have not yet permanently departed from the perspective of the transformation-body;

if, however, they have already begun to erode the specific afflictions within the birth-body, they are considered to have permanently departed from the perspective of the residual [afflictions] within the transformation-body.

Next, to explain the contemplation of the three poisons through the method of inverse exposition: all sentient beings are said to possess "few desires" [in this context] because they cease the anger that leads to the suffering of the three miserable realms and instead crave the pleasures of the human and celestial worlds. As for delusion, it is likewise understood through this inverse perspective.
The followers of the Two Vehicles merely loathe birth-and-death and desire to attain the bliss of nirvana; thus, they are all said to be "small. Bodhisattvas are not like this:

they joyfully seek the Buddha-dharma, seeking not merely one aspect of the Buddha-dharma, but universally seeking all unspeakable Buddha-dharmas, just as the ocean swallows all streams yet remains never full. They neither accept birth-and-death nor do they accept nirvana; therefore, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of the "five non-acceptances," which is precisely what constitutes "great loathing."
The power of ignorance is great, and only the Buddha’s wisdom can sever it; yet for the Bodhisattva, the delusion of ignorance remains a force of great power.
Furthermore, delusion is like space and cannot be exhausted, and so on until old age and death, which are like space and cannot be exhausted.
These three poisons are themselves three Dharma-gates:
first, grasping; second, relinquishing; third, neither grasping nor relinquishing.

Great kindness and great compassion, the four means of integration, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, samādhis, liberations, unsurpassed bodhi, purifying buddha-lands, and transforming and delivering sentient beings—these are called the gate of grasping, which is precisely great greed.
All dharmas are empty and non-existent; they neither abide nor are they attached to.
Prajñā is like a great conflagration, which cannot be grasped from any of its four sides.

Great Nirvāṇa is empty, and the city of Kapilavastu is empty; the path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. One does not attain Bodhi by means of the four propositions; this state of neither attainment nor realization is the gate of relinquishment, and it is called "Great Anger."

The Middle Way is neither grasping nor abandoning; it is without aversion and without attachment, without annihilation and without permanence, without going and without coming, and without arising and without ceasing. Like a reflection in a mirror, it is seen though it cannot be seen; it is seen yet cannot be seen. It is neither visible nor invisible, for it excludes the two extremes. Thus, it is ineffable; even the silence of Vimalakīrti is called the Middle Way, and this is precisely what is meant by "great delusion."
Therefore, Mañjuśrī said:
"I am the śrī of desire, the śrī of hatred, and the śrī of wrong views.
This is the clear evidence of it.

If one wishes to fulfill these three dharma-gates, by constantly mindfuly recollecting Avalokiteśvara, all vows will be fulfilled. Whether a sage practices for themselves or transforms others, there is nothing that does not enter through these three gates; apart from these, there is no other path.
Thus, the *Caryā-apratipatti Sūtra* says:
"Desire itself is the path; so too are hatred and delusion. Within these three dharmas, all the Buddha-dharmas are fully contained."

"All Buddha-dharmas do not transcend the ten thousand practices of the pāramitās, the vast function of samādhi-reception, and the true mark of the Middle Way. These three dharma-gates cannot be fully proclaimed; yet, out of compassion for sentient beings, they may be taught either in accordance with or in opposition to [the listener's capacity], with various elements being adopted or rejected. As stated in the forty-second fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "In the city of Ratnavyūha in the perilous land of Khaṇḍarīka, the woman Vasumitrā expounded the Dharma-gate of the Limit of Freedom from Desire:

The vows and practices are as stated in the text. Regarding "virtue and action":

a man of refinement possesses a hundred types of conduct, of which wisdom is foremost. If one possesses only wisdom but lacks merit, then one’s status will be low and one’s wealth meager, encountering obstacles at every turn.

In the "Seeking a Wife" (Qiunü) chapter, only the vows and virtuous deeds are clarified while the practices are not; since the practice is identical to that of the *Lībái* (Prostration), it is not discussed again.

A woman’s physical comeliness is the foremost of the seven virtues. However, if one possesses comeliness but lacks auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*), she may become orphaned at an early age or widowed young, as her fortune indicated by those marks is not favorable.

"If one's affection is accompanied by pride, how can it be called a virtue?
To love and revere [the teacher] is precisely what constitutes this mark.
Someone explains it thus:

The multitude all said:

If you argue that one fears falling into causelessness regarding merit, why do you not fear falling into causelessness regarding birth?
If that were so, the Noble One would be entirely unable to bestow merit and wisdom, and could only act as a matchmaker.
This is difficult to understand.

If it were difficult for Avalokiteśvara to bestow merit and wisdom upon a child, then why is it that when one person calls his name, many people are all liberated from the peril of the rākṣasas? If there is no cause, he would not grant it to them; if there is no capacity, why are they suddenly liberated?

Now it is explained that the power of the Sage is exceedingly great and nothing is beyond its reach; it can cause those who possessed merit and wisdom in previous lives to take rebirth. If there is prostration, the merit will not be in vain; this forms the basis for the formation of bodily karma, and it also serves to resolve doubts.
The meaning of this formulation can be understood.

"Vain" (*táng*) means empty; "in vain" (*tuánjiān*) means discarded. This occurs because the mind lacks resolve, and thus the vow remains unfulfilled. Nevertheless, the merit of the prostration is not lost as it provides subtle, hidden support. This constitutes the resolution of the doubt.

These males and females do not require laborious seeking through vows; they spontaneously form a retinue.
If secular texts regard Heaven as Yang and Earth as Yin, and stillness and movement as male and female, how much more so must this be the case in the Buddha-dharma?
If one takes the Buddha as the King and the scriptural teachings as the Queen, they give birth to all Bodhisattvas and sons of the Buddha.
Furthermore, skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) is the father, and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the mother; all teachers of humanity are born from these two.
